The board should separate “uranium risk” into four linked but different markets: mined uranium, conversion, enrichment, and fuel fabrication. Mining produces uranium concentrate, but it must be converted into uranium hexafluoride, enriched to the reactor’s required isotope level, reconverted and fabricated into reactor-specific fuel assemblies before it can generate electricity. For today’s conventional reactors, the main mining risk is a slow, concentrated supply response rather than an immediate geological shortage, because Kazakhstan is the largest producer, existing inventories have been drawn down, and new-reactor demand is expected to increase. That means a mine disruption normally appears first as higher prices and tighter contracting, whereas a failure in conversion, enrichment or fabrication can become a physical scheduling problem even when uranium concentrate is available. Conversion is especially important because only a small number of facilities perform the technically specialized step from milled uranium to uranium hexafluoride, and Russia has historically supplied a large share of that capacity. Enrichment is a separate concentration risk, with the retrieved evidence attributing roughly 43% of global enrichment capacity to Russia, followed by Europe, China and the United States. Fuel fabrication is less exposed to a single global commodity price, but it is not instantly interchangeable because fuel assemblies are engineered for particular reactor designs and qualified manufacturing routes. Russia therefore matters not only because of Russian uranium mines, but because Kazakh material may transit Russian infrastructure and because Russian companies have occupied important positions in conversion, enrichment, reactor supply and fuel supply. China is a different kind of risk: its expanding reactor fleet can increase competition for Kazakh uranium and other available material, while its own fuel-cycle expansion makes it a major strategic buyer and, for advanced fuel, another country with production capability. The practical conclusion is that a conventional reactor does not face a “Russia or no electricity” binary, but a Russian disruption could still raise costs, delay replacement contracts, or expose a utility to conversion and enrichment bottlenecks if its procurement chain is geographically concentrated. HALEU is materially more exposed than ordinary reactor fuel because it is enriched above 5% and below 20% uranium-235, is required by several proposed advanced-reactor designs, and was not commercially available from US suppliers at the time of the retrieved evidence. The HALEU problem is therefore not simply a higher uranium price; it is the need to create qualified enrichment and fuel-production capacity before a large commercial reactor fleet exists to support it. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed that vulnerability because early US advanced-reactor projects expected to source their HALEU from Russia, while government inventories of highly enriched uranium were considered as a temporary feedstock for diluted HALEU. For a board considering an SMR, the decisive question should be whether the proposed design has a credible, contracted, non-Russian HALEU pathway by the date fuel is needed, not merely whether the vendor has a reactor license or a uranium-mining memorandum. Uranium price spikes are economically serious but do not translate one-for-one into power-price spikes, because utilities commonly buy through multi-year contracts and can hold inventories, while the uranium component is only one stage of the complete fuel cost. Price risk remains real because financial buying, reduced inventories, mine underinvestment, rising reactor demand and competition for long-term material can all tighten the market before a physical shortage occurs. Long-term contracting helps in three ways: it reserves future material, gives mines and fuel-cycle suppliers the revenue certainty needed to finance capacity, and reduces dependence on volatile spot purchases. It does not eliminate risk, because a contract may cover uranium concentrate but not conversion, enrichment or fabrication, may rely on a supplier’s ability to perform, may contain escalation or market-linked pricing, and may still route through a politically exposed country. Long-term contracts can also be expensive insurance, since historical utility contracts have sometimes been priced materially above contemporaneous spot prices, so the board should evaluate the avoided outage and replacement-procurement risk rather than treating a low headline uranium price as the benchmark. The board should separate “uranium risk” into four linked but different markets: mined uranium, conversion, enrichment, and fuel fabrication. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_01401_49505]

Mining produces uranium concentrate, but it must be converted into uranium hexafluoride, enriched to the reactor’s required isotope level, reconverted and fabricated into reactor-specific fuel assemblies before it can generate electricity. [shard_04764_4126]

For today’s conventional reactors, the main mining risk is a slow, concentrated supply response rather than an immediate geological shortage, because Kazakhstan is the largest producer, existing inventories have been drawn down, and new-reactor demand is expected to increase. [shard_04029_80802] [shard_03198_49172]

That means a mine disruption normally appears first as higher prices and tighter contracting, whereas a failure in conversion, enrichment or fabrication can become a physical scheduling problem even when uranium concentrate is available. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_04764_4126]

Conversion is especially important because only a small number of facilities perform the technically specialized step from milled uranium to uranium hexafluoride, and Russia has historically supplied a large share of that capacity. [shard_04912_28668]

Enrichment is a separate concentration risk, with the retrieved evidence attributing roughly 43% of global enrichment capacity to Russia, followed by Europe, China and the United States. [shard_04912_28668]

Fuel fabrication is less exposed to a single global commodity price, but it is not instantly interchangeable because fuel assemblies are engineered for particular reactor designs and qualified manufacturing routes. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_04764_4126]

Russia therefore matters not only because of Russian uranium mines, but because Kazakh material may transit Russian infrastructure and because Russian companies have occupied important positions in conversion, enrichment, reactor supply and fuel supply. [shard_04912_28668]

China is a different kind of risk: its expanding reactor fleet can increase competition for Kazakh uranium and other available material, while its own fuel-cycle expansion makes it a major strategic buyer and, for advanced fuel, another country with production capability. [shard_04029_80802] [shard_01801_1835] [shard_04702_36184]

The practical conclusion is that a conventional reactor does not face a “Russia or no electricity” binary, but a Russian disruption could still raise costs, delay replacement contracts, or expose a utility to conversion and enrichment bottlenecks if its procurement chain is geographically concentrated. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_03198_49172]

HALEU is materially more exposed than ordinary reactor fuel because it is enriched above 5% and below 20% uranium-235, is required by several proposed advanced-reactor designs, and was not commercially available from US suppliers at the time of the retrieved evidence. [shard_04702_36184]

The HALEU problem is therefore not simply a higher uranium price; it is the need to create qualified enrichment and fuel-production capacity before a large commercial reactor fleet exists to support it. [shard_02768_44044]

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed that vulnerability because early US advanced-reactor projects expected to source their HALEU from Russia, while government inventories of highly enriched uranium were considered as a temporary feedstock for diluted HALEU. [shard_02508_35653] [shard_02213_69231]

For a board considering an SMR, the decisive question should be whether the proposed design has a credible, contracted, non-Russian HALEU pathway by the date fuel is needed, not merely whether the vendor has a reactor license or a uranium-mining memorandum. [shard_04702_36184] [shard_02213_69231]

Uranium price spikes are economically serious but do not translate one-for-one into power-price spikes, because utilities commonly buy through multi-year contracts and can hold inventories, while the uranium component is only one stage of the complete fuel cost. [shard_03095_68102] [shard_03813_66082]

Price risk remains real because financial buying, reduced inventories, mine underinvestment, rising reactor demand and competition for long-term material can all tighten the market before a physical shortage occurs. [shard_01091_51633] [shard_04029_80802]

Long-term contracting helps in three ways: it reserves future material, gives mines and fuel-cycle suppliers the revenue certainty needed to finance capacity, and reduces dependence on volatile spot purchases. [shard_03095_68102] [shard_05859_29939]

It does not eliminate risk, because a contract may cover uranium concentrate but not conversion, enrichment or fabrication, may rely on a supplier’s ability to perform, may contain escalation or market-linked pricing, and may still route through a politically exposed country. [shard_01401_49505] [shard_04912_28668]

Long-term contracts can also be expensive insurance, since historical utility contracts have sometimes been priced materially above contemporaneous spot prices, so the board should evaluate the avoided outage and replacement-procurement risk rather than treating a low headline uranium price as the benchmark. [shard_01080_8935]

A credible power-purchase agreement should therefore require the generator or vendor to disclose its complete fuel bill of materials, named mines, conversion plants, enrichment providers, fabricators, transport routes, inventory policy and replacement suppliers. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_04912_28668]

The contract should assign responsibility for every stage, prohibit excessive dependence on one country or one facility, require minimum forward fuel coverage, and provide remedies if a supplier loses export authorization, qualification, capacity or transport access. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_01757_32476]

The board should also require price transparency across uranium, conversion, enrichment, fabrication, transport and storage, with separate caps or adjustment formulas instead of accepting a single opaque “fuel pass-through” charge. [shard_01080_8935] [shard_03095_68102]

For a conventional large reactor with a diversified supply chain, several years of forward contracting and inventory, nuclear fuel risk looks more like a manageable procurement and geopolitical exposure than a gas-style immediate fuel crisis. [shard_03095_68102] [shard_03813_66082] [shard_03198_49172]

For an SMR or advanced reactor dependent on HALEU, the risk is substantially higher until commercial non-Russian enrichment and fabrication capacity is operating at meaningful scale. [shard_02768_44044] [shard_04702_36184]

The sensible decision rule is not to reject nuclear because uranium prices are volatile, but to make the project conditional on a fully financed, diversified and contractually enforceable fuel pathway, with a conventional-reactor proposal treated as procurement-manageable and an HALEU proposal treated as contingent on successful fuel-market build-out.
